diamond_model_summary: The incident involves the use of agentic AI by adversaries to conduct autonomous cyber operations. The AI tools enable both entry-level and experienced threat actors to execute sophisticated attacks without requiring technical expertise. The adversary's capability includes AI-driven reconnaissance, social engineering, and exploitation, posing a high threat to potential victims. doc_summary: The text discusses the evolution of artificial intelligence (AI) in cyber offense, highlighting the transition from AI as an assistant to agentic AI capable of autonomous operations. It emphasizes the implications of AI-driven tools for entry-level threat actors, enabling them to conduct sophisticated attacks without technical expertise. The text also explores the impact on experienced practitioners, who benefit from increased operational speed. Key topics include AI-assisted reconnaissance, social engineering, vulnerability discovery, and malware development. The text warns of the challenges posed by AI's ability to erase traditional phishing signals and the need for robust defenses. It mentions the SANS SEC535 course, which covers offensive AI techniques, and the role of AI in the broader cybersecurity landscape.

Title: Malicious npm Packages Deliver Windows RAT

Victim.Description: Developers using npm packages were targeted.

diamond_model_summary: The incident involves a North Korean adversary using malicious npm packages to deliver a Windows-based RAT. The adversary's capability includes using JavaScript droppers and PowerShell scripts to deploy the RAT, which communicates with a C2 server. The infrastructure involves domains and IPs for payload delivery and C2 communication. Victims are developers using npm packages, with a high impact severity due to credential theft and data exfiltration.
doc_summary: Cybersecurity researchers discovered malicious npm packages designed to deliver a Windows-based remote access trojan (RAT). The packages, published by an npm user named 'abdrizak', include 'Aes-decode-runner-pro', 'postcss-minify-selector-parser', and 'postcss-minify-selector'. These packages deploy a JavaScript dropper that writes a PowerShell script to disk, which downloads a payload from 'nvidiadriver[.]net'. The payload includes a Visual Basic Script and a Python runtime, which set up the environment for the RAT. The RAT gathers host information, siphons credentials from Google Chrome, and communicates with a C2 server at '95.216.92[.]207:8080'. This attack coincides with other campaigns targeting the npm ecosystem and overlaps with a North Korean operation dubbed PolinRider, which injects obfuscated JavaScript into GitHub repositories to deliver malware.
kill_chain_summary: The attack follows a structured kill chain: reconnaissance to identify npm packages, weaponization by creating malicious packages, delivery through npm, installation of the RAT via PowerShell scripts, command and control through a C2 server, and actions on objectives including credential theft and data exfiltration. The adversary's use of legitimate tools and obfuscation techniques complicates detection and remediation efforts.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes IP addresses and domain names used for C2 communication, as well as tools like PowerShell and Visual Basic scripts. The adversary's use of legitimate technologies and obfuscation techniques increases the difficulty of detection and response. The RAT's capabilities for credential theft and data exfiltration pose significant challenges for defenders.

doc_summary: A malicious campaign is using WhatsApp to distribute VBScript files that install Remote Monitoring and Management (RMM) software. The campaign targets WhatsApp Desktop and Web users in countries like Malaysia, Brazil, India, and others. The VBScript files are disguised as business documents and contain comments mimicking Windows Update components. The infection chain involves downloading additional VBScript components and tampering with Windows User Account Control. The campaign's infrastructure overlaps with Gh0st RAT and ValleyRAT activities. Kaspersky advises caution with unexpected attachments, especially VBS, VBE, EXE, BAT, CMD, JS, and PS1 files.

Title: Malware Campaign Targeting WhatsApp Users with VBScript Files

Victim.Description: WhatsApp users in multiple countries are targeted.
Victim.Geography: Brazil, India, Mexico, Singapore, United Kingdom, Spain, Taiwan, Australia, Russia, Vietnam, Malaysia

diamond_model_summary: The adversary targets WhatsApp users globally, using VBScript files disguised as financial documents to gain remote access. The campaign exploits compromised WhatsApp accounts to deliver malware, installing ManageEngine Endpoint Central for remote administration. The infrastructure includes attacker-controlled servers, with signs of Chinese language use and overlap with ValleyRAT and Gh0st RAT activity.
doc_summary: An ongoing malware campaign is targeting WhatsApp users in multiple countries with deceptive messages that push VBScript files, leading to remote system access. The threat actor uses file names indicating business and financial documents delivered by compromised contacts. By downloading and executing the malicious attachments, the infection chain installs ManageEngine Endpoint Central, used by IT administrators to manage systems. The campaign spreads across Brazil, India, Mexico, Singapore, the United Kingdom, Spain, Taiwan, Australia, Russia, Vietnam, and Malaysia. The attacks begin with messages from compromised accounts containing heavily obfuscated VBS files. These files appear as financial reports, billing statements, and account notices. The filenames are localized in multiple languages, confirming the campaign's global reach. The exact method used to compromise WhatsApp accounts remains unknown. The VBScript fetches additional scripts, disables UAC protections, and downloads a ZIP archive containing ManageEngine Endpoint Central. The software is installed and configured to connect to attacker-controlled servers, giving remote administration access. Signs of Chinese language use and infrastructure overlap with ValleyRAT and Gh0st RAT activity were found, but attribution is uncertain. WhatsApp users are advised to treat files with caution and verify them through secondary means.
kill_chain_summary: The attack begins with reconnaissance to identify potential targets, followed by weaponization of VBScript files. Delivery occurs via WhatsApp messages from compromised accounts. Exploitation relies on user execution of the malicious files, leading to installation of ManageEngine Endpoint Central. Command and control is achieved through attacker-controlled servers, enabling remote access to victim systems.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes VBScript files and ManageEngine Endpoint Central as tools, with potential overlap with ValleyRAT and Gh0st RAT infrastructure. The campaign's global reach and use of compromised WhatsApp accounts increase the difficulty of detection and response. The lack of specific indicators such as hashes or IP addresses limits the ability to disrupt the adversary's operations.

Title: FortiBleed Campaign Targets Fortinet FortiGate Devices

Victim.Description: The campaign targets organizations using Fortinet FortiGate devices worldwide.

diamond_model_summary: The FortiBleed campaign involves a sophisticated adversary using custom tools to target Fortinet FortiGate devices. The adversary acts as an initial access broker, employing credential stuffing and brute-force attacks to gain access. The campaign leverages the FortigateSniffer tool to capture and analyze network traffic, extracting credentials for further exploitation. The infrastructure includes compromised FortiGate devices and a distributed GPU cluster for password cracking. Victims are organizations worldwide using Fortinet devices, with a high impact severity due to the potential for widespread credential compromise.
doc_summary: The FortiBleed campaign, as reported by SOCRadar, targets Fortinet FortiGate devices using custom sniffers to harvest authentication secrets. The operation, active since February 2026, involves credential stuffing, brute-force attacks, and offline password cracking to gain access to corporate networks. The attackers use a Golang-based tool, FortigateSniffer, to capture authentication traffic from compromised devices, targeting protocols like RADIUS, NTLM, Kerberos, and LDAP. The campaign involves processing captured data through SNIFTRAN and a Python-based toolkit to extract credentials, which are then cracked using Hashcat on a distributed GPU cluster. The threat actors also download FortiGate configuration files to obtain hashed credentials for cracking.
kill_chain_summary: The FortiBleed campaign follows a structured kill chain, beginning with reconnaissance to identify vulnerable FortiGate devices. The adversary weaponizes the FortigateSniffer tool to capture network traffic, delivering it through credential stuffing and brute-force attacks. Exploitation occurs via the FortiOS diagnose sniffer packet command, allowing the adversary to capture credentials. Installation involves deploying the FortigateSniffer tool on compromised devices, with command and control achieved through SSH. Actions on objectives include extracting and cracking credentials using Hashcat, highlighting the campaign's focus on credential access and exploitation.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The FortiBleed campaign presents significant challenges across the Pyramid of Pain. The use of custom tools like FortigateSniffer and the deployment of a distributed GPU cluster for password cracking indicate a high level of sophistication. The campaign's reliance on credential harvesting and network sniffing techniques further complicates detection and response efforts. While specific hash values, IP addresses, and domain names are not detailed, the campaign's focus on credential access and exploitation underscores the need for robust detection and remediation strategies. The adversary's ability to adapt and leverage advanced tools poses a persistent threat to targeted organizations.

Title: Supply Chain Attack on ShapedPlugin WordPress Plugins

Victim.Description: Site owners using ShapedPlugin's Pro plugins via Easy Digital Downloads.

diamond_model_summary: The supply chain attack on ShapedPlugin involved unknown threat actors compromising the vendor's build and distribution pipeline. The adversary injected backdoor code into Pro plugin releases, affecting site owners who installed updates from the official system. The attack utilized a remote server for payload delivery, and the malware was capable of capturing credentials and 2FA codes. The incident highlights the risks associated with supply chain compromises and the need for robust security measures in software distribution processes.
doc_summary: A supply chain attack compromised multiple WordPress plugins from ShapedPlugin, affecting Pro plugin builds distributed via Easy Digital Downloads. The attack involved injecting backdoor code into the vendor's build and distribution pipeline, leading to the installation of a fake plugin capable of capturing credentials and 2FA codes. The incident has been assigned CVE-2026-49777 and CVE-2026-10735, with CVSS scores of 10.0 and 9.8, respectively. The malware fetches a payload from a remote server, installs it, and activates it as a fake plugin, reporting the victim domain back to the server. ShapedPlugin is reviewing its processes to ensure product integrity, and affected site owners are advised to reset passwords, regenerate 2FA secrets, and review administrator accounts.
kill_chain_summary: The attack on ShapedPlugin's WordPress plugins followed a structured kill chain. Initially, the adversary compromised the vendor's build pipeline, injecting backdoor code into plugin releases. The compromised plugins were delivered via official update channels, leading to the installation of a fake plugin on victim sites. The malware established a command and control channel with a remote server, capturing credentials and 2FA codes. The attack demonstrates the effectiveness of supply chain compromises in achieving unauthorized access and data theft.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes several indicators. The IP address 194.76.217.28 was used for command and control communication. The domain account.shapedplugin.com was involved in the distribution of compromised plugins. The malware utilized a file named install-persistent.php for persistence. These indicators highlight the adversary's reliance on specific infrastructure and tools, which can be used to detect and mitigate similar attacks in the future.

Title: Underground Credential Search Services Exploitation

Victim.Description: Organizations and individuals targeted for credential theft and account takeovers.

diamond_model_summary: The incident involves threat actors operating as credential brokers in underground markets. They provide search services for stolen credentials, acting as a processing layer between infostealer infections and account takeovers. These actors are motivated by financial gain and leverage existing data from infostealers to offer targeted credential data to buyers.
doc_summary: Threat actors are increasingly using infostealer-derived credential collections to create underground services. These services allow buyers to request credentials for specific targets, such as companies or platforms. Researchers analyzed 470 forum posts from January 2025 to June 2026, revealing a service layer between infections and account takeovers. The actors involved are often Malware-as-a-Service providers or consumers, acting as credential brokers. They monetize logs by searching, filtering, and delivering targeted results. This service model aligns with MITRE ATT&CK techniques T1589.001 and T1650. Sellers advertise database sizes and search capabilities, but customer feedback indicates issues with data validity and duplication. The market overlaps with initial access brokers, posing risks to businesses. Defenders must monitor these markets to protect against credential-based attacks.
kill_chain_summary: The kill chain involves threat actors gathering credentials through infostealer infections, processing and enriching the data, and offering search services in underground markets. Buyers use these services to acquire credentials for specific targets, leading to account takeovers and other malicious activities. doc_summary: A vulnerability chain named AutoJack was discovered in Microsoft's AutoGen Studio, a component for prototyping AI agents. This vulnerability could allow attackers to manipulate an AI agent into executing arbitrary commands on its host system by visiting a malicious webpage. AutoGen Studio is part of Microsoft's open-source framework for building multi-agent AI systems. The issue was identified and remediated before any PyPI release, limiting exposure to developers who built AutoGen Studio from the main GitHub branch during a specific window. The attack involves a malicious JavaScript executing on a page visited by a developer's AI agent, opening a WebSocket connection to AutoGen Studio's local MCP endpoint, and launching an attacker-chosen command. Microsoft recommends deploying AutoGen Studio in an isolated environment and running it under a low-privilege account to contain any future agent-driven RCE.
kill_chain_summary: The AutoJack vulnerability involves several stages of the MITRE ATT&CK kill chain, including exploitation through a malicious webpage and execution of arbitrary commands on the host system. doc_summary: A vulnerability named Squidbleed (CVE-2026-47729) was discovered in the Squid web proxy, allowing a heap over-read that can leak cleartext HTTP requests, including credentials, to an attacker with proxy access. The bug originates from a 1997 FTP-parsing change and affects Squid's default configuration. The vulnerability is exploitable by a trusted client on shared networks like schools and offices. The attacker needs to control an FTP server on port 21, which is enabled by default. The issue lies in Squid's FTP directory-listing parser, where a loop fails to terminate correctly, leading to memory leakage. Researchers at Calif.io disclosed the vulnerability in June 2023, and proof-of-concept code is available. The recommended mitigation is to disable FTP in Squid configurations. The vulnerability is rated medium severity with a CVSS score of 6.5, as it requires low privileges and impacts confidentiality only.
kill_chain_summary: The Squidbleed vulnerability follows a structured kill chain, starting with reconnaissance to identify vulnerable Squid proxies. The attacker then weaponizes by setting up an FTP server to exploit the vulnerability. Delivery involves using the FTP server to deliver the exploit to the Squid proxy. Exploitation occurs when the attacker triggers the heap over-read vulnerability. Actions on objectives involve retrieving leaked HTTP requests and credentials. The vulnerability is rated medium severity, with a CVSS score of 6.5, impacting confidentiality.

diamond_model_summary: The REF8372 campaign involves a Russian-speaking threat actor using OXLOADER to deliver CastleStealer via malicious Google Ads. The infrastructure includes fake websites and abuse of the Storj platform. Victims are targeted through misleading ads, with a focus on non-CIS regions. doc_summary: Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed a new campaign delivering CastleStealer via OXLOADER. Elastic Security Labs identified the campaign leveraging malicious Google Ads to distribute malware. The threat actor is likely Russian-speaking and financially motivated, avoiding CIS regions. The campaign, codenamed REF8372, uses obfuscation, self-modifying decryption, and Windows .reloc section abuse. Users searching for 'lts version of node.js' are redirected to a fake site, node-js.prentiva99.info, via ads under the name 'ВОЛОДИМИР ТЕРЕЩЕНКО'. The site serves a batch script hosted on Storj, downloading OXLOADER through PowerShell. The attack uses DLL side-loading to execute CastleStealer. OXLOADER employs control-flow flattening and mixed Boolean-Arithmetic to evade detection. CastleStealer, a .NET information stealer, was distributed with CastleLoader in a campaign called BackgroundFix. OXLOADER's engineering suggests it is in an early operational phase, with low detection rates.
kill_chain_summary: The attack begins with reconnaissance using Google Ads to identify potential victims. Weaponization involves preparing OXLOADER with obfuscation techniques. Delivery is achieved through malicious ads redirecting to a fake website. Exploitation occurs when users run a batch script downloading OXLOADER. Installation uses DLL side-loading to execute CastleStealer. Command and Control is established via web protocols, and Actions on Objectives involve data exfiltration.

Victim.Security_Posture: Varied, with some regions having low cybersecurity maturity.

diamond_model_summary: The incident involves organized crime syndicates in Asia and the South Pacific leveraging advanced technologies like AI and deepfakes to conduct cybercrime. Their capabilities include phishing, ransomware, and social engineering, targeting sectors such as real estate, manufacturing, and financial services. The infrastructure includes extensive scam centers, and the victims are primarily in regions with low cybersecurity maturity.
doc_summary: INTERPOL's report highlights a dramatic increase in cybercrime in Asia and the South Pacific, driven by digitalization and organized crime. Phishing is the most damaging cybercrime, with over 10,000 cases reported in a third of countries. Cybercriminals use AI, ransomware-as-a-service, and social engineering. Ransomware attacks surged, impacting real estate, manufacturing, and financial services. Organized crime syndicates in Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, and the Philippines use forced labor for scams. Deepfake scams in Myanmar, Cambodia, and Laos caused $37 billion in losses. INTERPOL supports regional law enforcement with joint operations, training, and policy creation to enhance cyber resilience.
kill_chain_summary: The cybercriminals conduct reconnaissance using social engineering to gather victim information. They weaponize by creating phishing emails and deepfake content. Delivery is achieved through phishing and social engineering. Exploitation involves exploiting human vulnerabilities. Installation includes deploying ransomware. Command and control are established for data exfiltration. Actions on objectives involve data theft and financial fraud.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes TTPs such as phishing, ransomware, and social engineering, which are challenging to change. No specific hashes, IPs, or domains were identified, indicating a focus on behavioral indicators. The use of AI and deepfakes adds complexity to detection and response efforts, emphasizing the need for advanced threat intelligence and monitoring capabilities.

Title: AryStinger Malware Exploits Forgotten Routers for Reconnaissance Network

Victim.Description: The primary victims are users of outdated routers and NAS devices, particularly in South Korea and China.
Victim.Geography: South Korea, China, Sweden, Malaysia, Singapore

diamond_model_summary: AryStinger is a sophisticated malware campaign targeting outdated routers and NAS devices to create a distributed reconnaissance network. The adversary exploits known vulnerabilities in Realtek RTL819X-based routers and QNAP NAS devices, using them for internet scanning and traffic tunneling. The infrastructure includes compromised devices communicating with C2 servers over HTTP/HTTPS. The campaign primarily affects devices in South Korea and China, with a significant portion of infections in D-Link DIR-850L routers. The adversary remains unidentified, but the strategic use of forgotten hardware and ancient CVEs suggests a high level of sophistication.
doc_summary: AryStinger is a new malware family identified by QiAnXin's XLab, targeting forgotten home routers and QNAP NAS boxes. It exploits vulnerabilities CVE-2013-3307 in Linksys and CVE-2016-5681 in D-Link routers, as well as CVE-2025-11837 in QNAP NAS. The malware turns these devices into a distributed reconnaissance and proxy network, scanning the internet, fingerprinting services, and tunneling traffic. The campaign primarily affects routers with Realtek RTL819X chips, with a significant number of infections in South Korea and China. The malware uses a Dropbear SSH server for persistence and communicates with its C2 over HTTP/HTTPS. The attack was first observed on March 12, 2026, spreading from IP 107.150.106.14. The malware's infrastructure includes domains like ajb8.com, and it employs tools such as fscan, ksubdomain, and httpx for reconnaissance.
kill_chain_summary: The AryStinger campaign follows a structured kill chain, beginning with reconnaissance through internet scanning and service fingerprinting. Exploitation occurs via known vulnerabilities in outdated routers and NAS devices, leading to the installation of malware for persistence. Command and control is established through HTTP/HTTPS communication with C2 servers, using obfuscated traffic. The final stage involves actions on objectives, where compromised devices are used for footprinting and traffic tunneling. The campaign demonstrates a strategic use of outdated hardware and vulnerabilities to establish a distributed reconnaissance network.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The AryStinger campaign presents several indicators across the Pyramid of Pain. IP addresses like 107.150.106.14 and domains such as ajb8.com are used for C2 communication. The malware employs tools like fscan, ksubdomain, and httpx for reconnaissance. Known vulnerabilities CVE-2013-3307, CVE-2016-5681, and CVE-2025-11837 are exploited for initial access. The use of Protobuf-encoded traffic obfuscated by XOR adds complexity to detection efforts. The campaign's reliance on outdated hardware and vulnerabilities highlights the importance of maintaining up-to-date security measures.

Title: AryStinger Botnet Compromises Outdated Routers

Victim.Description: Victims are primarily users of outdated D-Link routers and NAS systems.
Victim.Geography: South Korea, China, Sweden, Malaysia, Singapore
Victim.Security_Posture: Weak due to outdated hardware and software

diamond_model_summary: The AryStinger botnet incident involves an unidentified adversary exploiting outdated routers to create a botnet for malicious activities. The adversary's capability includes using the AryStinger malware to convert routers into executors for tasks like scanning and proxying. The infrastructure consists of compromised routers and NAS systems, with victims primarily located in South Korea, China, Sweden, Malaysia, and Singapore. The adversary's strategic objective is to leverage these compromised devices for malicious operations, including DNS tampering and network traffic monitoring.
doc_summary: AryStinger is a newly identified malware botnet that has compromised over 4,000 outdated routers, primarily targeting D-Link DIR-850L and DIR-818LW models. The malware exploits vulnerabilities such as CVE-2013-3307, CVE-2016-5681, and CVE-2025-11837. Researchers from Qianxin's XLab have observed that AryStinger converts infected devices into executors for malicious activities like scanning, proxying, and command execution. The botnet's infections are concentrated in South Korea, China, Sweden, Malaysia, and Singapore. AryStinger also has a Go-based variant targeting NAS systems, featuring advanced capabilities like IP and DNS scanning. The malware can tamper with DNS settings, hijack browsing, and monitor network traffic. Despite its capabilities, AryStinger has not been attributed to any known threat actor group. The researchers recommend replacing end-of-life routers, updating firmware, and securing administrator accounts to mitigate risks.
kill_chain_summary: The AryStinger botnet follows a structured kill chain, starting with reconnaissance through distributed scanning using compromised routers. Exploitation occurs via known vulnerabilities in outdated routers, leading to the installation of AryStinger malware. The command and control stage involves using compromised devices for command execution and control. Finally, actions on objectives include DNS tampering and network traffic monitoring. Detection and remediation efforts focus on monitoring for unusual activity, applying patches, and securing network configurations.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The AryStinger botnet incident lacks specific indicators like hashes, IPs, or domains, making it challenging to populate the Pyramid of Pain. However, the use of known vulnerabilities and the AryStinger malware itself are significant indicators. The incident highlights the importance of monitoring for unusual network activity and securing outdated devices to prevent exploitation. The absence of specific indicators limits the ability to provide a detailed Pyramid of Pain analysis.

Title: Prinz Eugen Ransomware Attack Analysis

Victim.Description: Organizations targeted by Prinz Eugen ransomware.

diamond_model_summary: The Prinz Eugen ransomware group employs hands-on-keyboard tactics, using legitimate RMM tools and living-off-the-land techniques to maximize impact on business-critical files. They gain initial access through stolen RDP credentials and maintain persistence with backdoor accounts. Their operations do not follow the ransomware-as-a-service model, and they avoid leaving ransom notes to reduce forensic footprints.
doc_summary: Prinz Eugen ransomware operation prioritizes recently modified files for encryption without leaving a ransom note. Threatdown, Malwarebytes' enterprise cybersecurity arm, discovered that the hackers use legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) software and living-off-the-land tools. Initial access is likely through stolen RDP credentials, followed by manual download and execution of 'servertool.exe'. The attack uses RemotePC RMM tool and a backdoor administrator account for persistence. Prinz Eugen does not operate under the ransomware-as-a-service model. The ransomware employs ChaCha20-Poly1305 encryption with a 32-byte master key, Argon2id, SHA-256, and HKDF-SHA256 for key derivation. The encryption process is carried out in 1 MB chunks, and file integrity is checked using SHA-256. The malware overwrites the encryption key with zeroes and self-deletes to prevent retrieval. No ransom note is dropped, reducing forensic footprint. The attack lists three victims on a data leak site, with more organizations impacted.
kill_chain_summary: The Prinz Eugen ransomware attack begins with gaining access through stolen RDP credentials, followed by the installation of 'servertool.exe' for ransomware execution. The attackers use legitimate RMM tools and backdoor accounts for persistence. The ransomware encrypts recently modified files using ChaCha20-Poly1305 encryption, prioritizing business-critical data to pressure victims into paying the ransom. The absence of a ransom note complicates detection of the extortion phase.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for the Prinz Eugen ransomware attack includes the use of specific tools like RemotePC and servertool.exe, as well as TTPs such as living-off-the-land techniques and data encryption for impact. The attackers' use of legitimate tools and advanced encryption methods increases the difficulty of detection and response. The absence of specific IP addresses, domains, or hashes in the available data limits the ability to track and block the attack effectively.

Title: Mastra AI Supply Chain Attack by Sapphire Sleet

Victim.Description: Developers and organizations using compromised npm packages.

diamond_model_summary: The Mastra AI supply chain attack attributed to Sapphire Sleet involved compromising npm packages to deploy malware. The adversary, a North Korean state-sponsored group, targeted the financial sector to steal credentials and cryptocurrency. The attack leveraged malicious npm updates, a cross-platform information stealer, and C2 infrastructure.
doc_summary: Microsoft has attributed a recent supply chain attack on Mastra AI, compromising over 140 npm packages, to the North Korean hacking group Sapphire Sleet, also known as BlueNoroff. The attack involved hijacking an npm maintainer account to publish malicious package updates, injecting a dependency named 'easy-day-js', a typosquat of the legitimate dayjs library. The malicious dependency executed a post-install hook deploying a malware dropper aimed at stealing sensitive credentials, API keys, authentication tokens, and cryptocurrency wallets. The second-stage payload was a cross-platform information stealer targeting Windows, Linux, and macOS systems, collecting host information, browser histories, installed applications, and checking for cryptocurrency wallet extensions. Persistence methods varied by OS, including Windows Registry Run keys, macOS LaunchAgents, and Linux systemd services. Follow-on activity included a PowerShell backdoor, additional persistence mechanisms, and a malicious Windows service granting SYSTEM privileges. Sapphire Sleet is known for targeting the financial sector with software supply chain compromises.
kill_chain_summary: The attack began with the compromise of an npm maintainer account, leading to the weaponization of a malicious dependency. Delivery occurred through npm package updates, exploiting the supply chain. Installation involved a malware dropper, followed by C2 communication. Actions on objectives included data collection and credential theft.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes TTPs such as supply chain compromise and credential theft. Tools like a PowerShell backdoor and persistence mechanisms were used. No specific hashes, IPs, or domains were identified, limiting the ability to disrupt the adversary's operations through traditional indicators.

Title: Exploitation of CVE-2026-4020 in Gravity SMTP Plugin

Victim.Description: WordPress sites using vulnerable Gravity SMTP plugin

diamond_model_summary: The incident involves threat actors exploiting CVE-2026-4020 in the Gravity SMTP plugin, affecting WordPress sites globally. The adversary's capability includes exploiting a REST API endpoint to extract sensitive data. The infrastructure involves unauthenticated HTTP GET requests to the vulnerable endpoint. Victims are WordPress sites using the vulnerable plugin, with data types at risk including configuration data and API keys.
doc_summary: Threat actors are exploiting a medium-severity vulnerability, CVE-2026-4020, in the Gravity SMTP WordPress plugin, affecting approximately 100,000 sites. This flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to extract sensitive data, including configuration data, API keys, secrets, and OAuth tokens, via a REST API endpoint. The vulnerability is due to a permission_callback that returns true, enabling access to the endpoint. Attackers can leverage this to harvest credentials and gain insights into the site's software stack, facilitating further attacks. A patch has been released in version 2.1.5 of the plugin. Wordfence has blocked over 17 million exploit attempts, with activity peaking in early June 2026. Site owners are advised to update the plugin, rotate credentials, and review server logs for suspicious activity.
kill_chain_summary: The attack begins with reconnaissance to identify vulnerable WordPress sites using the Gravity SMTP plugin. Exploitation occurs through CVE-2026-4020, allowing attackers to extract sensitive data via a REST API endpoint. Actions on objectives include harvesting credentials and planning further attacks. Detection involves monitoring for specific HTTP GET requests, and remediation includes updating the plugin and rotating credentials.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes IP addresses and TTPs. IP addresses are involved in the exploit attempts, while TTPs include exploiting a public-facing application vulnerability. The lack of specific hash values, domain names, and tools limits the pyramid's complexity. Monitoring HTTP GET requests and updating the plugin are key to mitigating the threat.

Title: Klue OAuth Token Theft by Icarus Extortion Group

Victim.Description: Organizations using Klue's Salesforce integrations were targeted, leading to data theft.

diamond_model_summary: The Icarus extortion group targeted Klue's integration infrastructure, exploiting compromised OAuth tokens to access Salesforce environments. The attackers used Python scripts to automate data exfiltration, focusing on business contacts and sales communications. The incident highlights the risks associated with third-party integrations and the need for robust credential management.
doc_summary: Klue, a market intelligence platform, confirmed a security incident involving the theft of OAuth tokens by the Icarus extortion group. The attackers accessed Salesforce environments through compromised Klue Battlecards integrations, leading to data theft from multiple organizations. Klue CEO Jason Smith stated the breach was discovered on June 12, involving unauthorized access via a legacy credential. The company revoked affected credentials, removed unauthorized code, and engaged CrowdStrike for response. ReliaQuest and Huntress identified the use of Python scripts to query Salesforce's API. The stolen data included business contacts and sales communications. Icarus publicly claimed responsibility, pressuring victims to contact them via Session messaging to prevent data leaks. The incident primarily affected third-party integrations, not Klue's platform directly. Organizations warned of potential phishing and extortion risks.
kill_chain_summary: The attack began with reconnaissance on Klue's integration infrastructure, followed by exploitation of compromised OAuth tokens to access Salesforce environments. The attackers automated data exfiltration using Python scripts, focusing on sensitive business data. The incident underscores the importance of securing third-party integrations and monitoring API access.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes the use of OAuth tokens and Python scripts as key indicators. The attackers' reliance on compromised credentials and API access highlights the need for robust monitoring and credential management. The incident demonstrates the challenges of detecting and mitigating attacks leveraging legitimate access methods.

Title: usbliter8 Exploit Targets Apple's A12 and A13 SecureROM

Victim.Description: Devices with A12 and A13 chips are vulnerable.
Victim.Security_Posture: Vulnerable due to unpatchable hardware flaw

diamond_model_summary: The usbliter8 exploit, developed by Paradigm Shift, targets Apple's A12 and A13 chips by exploiting a hardware flaw in the Synopsys DWC2 USB controller. The exploit requires physical access to the device in DFU mode and uses a specific microcontroller board to execute arbitrary code in SecureROM. Devices such as iPhone XS, iPhone 11, and Apple Watch Series 4 are affected. The vulnerability is unpatchable via software updates, making affected devices permanently vulnerable. The exploit was publicly disclosed on June 18, 2026, following coordinated disclosure with Apple.
doc_summary: Security researchers at Paradigm Shift have disclosed a working exploit named usbliter8 that allows arbitrary code execution in the SecureROM of Apple's A12 and A13 chips. This exploit requires physical access to the device, which must be in DFU mode and connected via USB to a specific microcontroller board. The vulnerability stems from a hardware flaw in the Synopsys DWC2 USB controller, which allows a buffer underflow to overwrite arbitrary SRAM due to Apple's configuration of the USB DART in SecureROM. The exploit affects devices such as iPhone XS, iPhone 11, iPad Air 3rd gen, and Apple Watch Series 4 and 5. The exploit cannot be patched via software updates, making affected devices permanently vulnerable. The public proof of concept was released on June 18, 2026, following coordinated disclosure with Apple. No CVE or CVSS score has been issued, and no in-the-wild exploitation has been reported. The practical risk is low for most users, but high-security environments should consider hardware refreshes to A14 or newer.
kill_chain_summary: The usbliter8 exploit follows a specific kill chain involving physical access to the target device, exploitation of a hardware flaw in the Synopsys DWC2 USB controller, and execution of arbitrary code in SecureROM. The exploit requires the device to be in DFU mode and connected to a specific microcontroller board. The vulnerability affects Apple's A12 and A13 chips, making devices such as iPhone XS and iPhone 11 permanently vulnerable. The exploit cannot be patched via software updates, posing a high risk to affected devices.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The usbliter8 exploit presents a significant challenge in terms of detection and mitigation due to its reliance on a hardware flaw in the Synopsys DWC2 USB controller. The exploit requires physical access to the device and specific hardware setup, making traditional detection methods ineffective. The vulnerability affects Apple's A12 and A13 chips, and the exploit cannot be patched via software updates. This places the exploit at a high level on the Pyramid of Pain, as it requires significant effort to detect and mitigate.

Title: FortiBleed Campaign Targets Fortinet Devices Globally

Victim.Description: Organizations using Fortinet devices across multiple sectors.
Victim.Geography: India, United States, Mexico, Colombia, Thailand
Victim.Security_Posture: Vulnerable due to poor password hygiene

diamond_model_summary: The FortiBleed campaign is a sophisticated attack attributed to Russian-speaking threat actors targeting Fortinet devices globally. The adversaries employ credential stuffing and brute-force attacks, exploiting poor password hygiene and legacy hashing mechanisms. The campaign impacts multiple sectors, including telecom, government, and education, with significant exposures in countries like India, the United States, and Mexico. The attackers have developed a bespoke tool for credential spraying, highlighting their high level of sophistication and capability.
doc_summary: The FortiBleed campaign, attributed to Russian-speaking threat actors, targets Fortinet devices globally, compromising 86,644 devices as of June 19, 2026. The attack exploits credential reuse and poor password hygiene, affecting sectors like telecom, government, and education, with significant exposures in India, the United States, Mexico, Colombia, and Thailand. The attackers use a bespoke tool for credential stuffing and brute-force attacks, leveraging older SHA-256 hashing mechanisms in FortiGate configurations. CISA and NCSC have issued advisories, urging organizations to rotate credentials and enable MFA. Fortinet has introduced PBKDF2-based hashing in newer FortiOS versions, but legacy credentials remain vulnerable. The incident highlights the importance of securing internet-facing devices and maintaining strong password policies.
kill_chain_summary: The FortiBleed campaign follows a structured kill chain, beginning with reconnaissance through mass scanning of Fortinet endpoints. The weaponization phase involves the development of a bespoke tool for credential spraying. Exploitation occurs through credential stuffing and brute-force attacks, leveraging legacy hashing mechanisms. The attackers achieve their objectives by harvesting credentials and building a verified database of working logins. The campaign demonstrates the importance of securing internet-facing devices and maintaining strong password policies.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The FortiBleed campaign presents challenges across the Pyramid of Pain, with the adversaries using legitimate credentials (TTPs) and bespoke tools for credential spraying. The attack exploits legacy hashing mechanisms, making it difficult to detect and remediate. The campaign highlights the importance of addressing credential reuse and poor password hygiene to disrupt adversary operations effectively.

Title: FortiBleed Data Leak Exposes 74,000 Fortinet Credentials

Victim.Description: Organizations using Fortinet devices, including government and private sectors.
Victim.Geography: Global, with high impact in India, United States, Taiwan, Mexico, Turkey, Thailand, Colombia, Malaysia, Chile, United Arab Emirates

diamond_model_summary: The FortiBleed incident involves threat actors exploiting compromised credentials to access Fortinet devices globally. The adversary's capability includes leveraging valid credentials to infiltrate systems, with the infrastructure comprising compromised Fortinet devices. Victims span multiple sectors, including telecommunications and healthcare, across various countries.
doc_summary: The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) issued a warning to Fortinet customers following the exposure of nearly 74,000 firewall and VPN credentials in a data leak known as 'FortiBleed'. Threat actors used compromised credentials to target internet-accessible Fortinet devices across government and private-sector organizations worldwide. The leak, uncovered by security researcher Volodymyr 'Bob' Diachenko, included valid Fortinet VPN credentials, usernames, email addresses, and plaintext passwords for 73,932 firewall URLs globally. The dataset also contained information on each organization's industry, revenue, and employee count. Hudson Rock described it as one of the largest known collections of compromised Fortinet credentials, spanning 21,632 unique domains and 194 countries. Notable organizations affected include Samsung, Mercedes-Benz, Foxconn, Chevron, Comcast, AT&T, and Toyota. The highest number of affected devices were from India, the United States, Taiwan, Mexico, Turkey, Thailand, Colombia, Malaysia, Chile, and the United Arab Emirates. The source of the data remains unknown, and it is unclear whether it was stolen through exploitation of previously disclosed Fortinet vulnerabilities, a newly discovered security flaw, or another method.
kill_chain_summary: The FortiBleed incident follows a kill chain where threat actors first gather credentials and organizational data (Reconnaissance), then exploit these credentials to access Fortinet devices (Exploitation). The potential for lateral movement and data exfiltration exists (Actions on Objectives), though specific details on other stages remain unclear.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The FortiBleed incident highlights the exposure of nearly 74,000 Fortinet credentials, posing a significant challenge in terms of detection and remediation. The lack of specific indicators such as hashes, IPs, or domains limits the ability to apply the Pyramid of Pain effectively. The focus remains on mitigating the impact of compromised credentials.

Title: Exploitation of Bluetooth Vulnerability in Beats Studio Buds

Victim.Description: Users of Beats Studio Buds wireless earbuds

diamond_model_summary: The incident involves a high-severity vulnerability in Beats Studio Buds, allowing unauthorized Bluetooth pairing and potential eavesdropping. The adversary could exploit the Airoha Bluetooth audio SDK flaw to gain remote escalation of privilege. The infrastructure exploited includes Bluetooth communication protocols, specifically Bluetooth BR/EDR and BLE. Victims are users of Beats Studio Buds, with the primary impact being unauthorized access to audio data.
doc_summary: Apple has patched a high-severity vulnerability in its Beats Studio Buds wireless earbuds, tracked as CVE-2025-20701, which could be exploited by nearby hackers to eavesdrop on users. The flaw, with a CVSS score of 8.8, involves incorrect authorization in the Airoha Bluetooth audio SDK, allowing unauthorized pairing of Bluetooth audio devices. Successful exploitation could lead to remote escalation of privilege without additional execution privileges or user interaction. The issue was addressed in Beats Firmware Update 1B211. Researchers Dennis Heinze and Frieder Steinmetz from ERNW GmbH disclosed the vulnerability in June 2025, alongside two other flaws in Airoha SoCs at the TROOPERS security conference in Germany. The vulnerabilities allow attackers to take over headphones via Bluetooth, with no authentication or pairing required, and can be triggered via Bluetooth BR/EDR or BLE. Attackers can read and write the device’s RAM and flash, hijacking trust relationships with other devices.
kill_chain_summary: The attack begins with the exploitation of a Bluetooth vulnerability (CVE-2025-20701) in Beats Studio Buds, allowing unauthorized access via Bluetooth. The adversary gains initial access through unauthorized pairing, leading to potential eavesdropping on audio data. The exploitation stage involves leveraging the incorrect authorization flaw in the Airoha Bluetooth audio SDK. The attack's primary objective is to capture audio data without user consent.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes the exploitation of a specific vulnerability (CVE-2025-20701) in Bluetooth communication protocols. The lack of specific hash values, IP addresses, or domain names limits the ability to track the adversary's actions. The primary TTP involves unauthorized Bluetooth pairing and audio capture, which are challenging to detect without specific indicators. The incident highlights the importance of securing Bluetooth communication channels.

diamond_model_summary: The ShapedPlugin supply chain attack involved a compromise of the build pipeline, allowing adversaries to distribute malicious updates to WordPress plugins. The adversary's capability included installing a fake plugin to impersonate WooCommerce components, steal credentials, and enable remote file-writing. The infrastructure involved a command-and-control server for managing the compromised plugins. Victims were users of ShapedPlugin's paid WordPress plugins, primarily in the technology sector.
doc_summary: In a supply chain attack, multiple WordPress plugins from ShapedPlugin were compromised, affecting three paid plugins: Product Slider Pro, Real Testimonials Pro, and Smart Post Show Pro. The attack involved a fake plugin impersonating WooCommerce components, stealing credentials, and enabling remote file-writing. The breach was identified by Wordfence, which found a malicious loader file contacting a C2 server. The attack was traced to a build pipeline compromise, with clean releases on WordPress.org. The incident is tracked under CVE-2026-10735. ShapedPlugin has implemented mitigation measures and is preparing updated releases.
kill_chain_summary: The attack on ShapedPlugin followed a structured kill chain, beginning with the weaponization of the build pipeline to inject malicious code into plugin updates. Delivery occurred through the official update system, leading to exploitation via a malicious loader file. Installation involved a fake plugin impersonating WooCommerce components. Command and control were established through a C2 server, and actions on objectives included credential theft and remote file-writing.

Title: International Operation Disrupts SocGholish Botnet and Evil Corp Infrastructure

Victim.Description: Nearly 15,000 WordPress websites were compromised by the SocGholish malware.

diamond_model_summary: The SocGholish botnet, operated by Evil Corp, targeted nearly 15,000 WordPress websites globally. The operation involved the use of JavaScript-based malware to hijack websites and distribute malicious payloads. The infrastructure included over 100 servers and domains, which were taken down by international law enforcement agencies. The victims were primarily website owners across various industries, with a high impact severity due to the widespread nature of the compromise.
doc_summary: International law enforcement agencies, including Europol and Eurojust, conducted a major operation targeting the SocGholish botnet and Evil Corp, a Russian cybercrime group. The operation involved cleaning nearly 15,000 malware-infected WordPress websites and taking down over 100 servers linked to the botnet. Authorities from the Netherlands, Canada, the United States, and Germany participated in the effort. The SocGholish malware, also known as FakeUpdates and GhoLoader, has been active since 2017, hijacking legitimate websites to trick visitors into downloading malicious payloads disguised as browser updates. The operation also targeted other malware families such as Dridex, Doppelpaymer, Empire, Koadic, Chtonic, and Azorult. The Dutch police advised website owners to change credentials, enable multi-factor authentication, and keep their sites updated. This marks the beginning of further actions against SocGholish.
kill_chain_summary: The SocGholish operation involved multiple stages of the MITRE ATT&CK kill chain. Initial access was gained through the exploitation of WordPress vulnerabilities, followed by the delivery of JavaScript-based malware disguised as browser updates. The malware established command and control channels using web protocols, allowing the adversary to deploy additional malware families. The operation was disrupted by law enforcement, who cleaned the infected websites and took down the associated infrastructure.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The operation against the SocGholish botnet involved various indicators of compromise, including domain names and network host artifacts. The disruption of over 100 servers and domains significantly impacted the adversary's operations. The use of JavaScript-based malware and the exploitation of WordPress vulnerabilities were key components of the attack. The pyramid of pain scoring reflects the complexity and impact of these indicators on the adversary's ability to conduct further operations.

doc_summary: Market intelligence platform Klue suffered an OAuth breach by the Icarus threat actors, leading to the theft of Salesforce CRM data from multiple organizations. The attack involved the use of OAuth tokens to query Salesforce's REST API, resulting in data exfiltration. Cybersecurity firms ReliaQuest and Huntress confirmed the incident, with Huntress stating their Salesforce data was stolen. Salesforce disabled the Klue Battlecards integration as a precaution. The attackers used automated scripts for data theft, and the extortion campaign involved emails with a Session Messenger ID. The breach impacted CRM-related information, but no evidence of compromised threat intelligence or payment data was found. The attack is attributed to the Icarus group, which launched in April 2026.

Title: INC Ransomware Group's Rise in 2026

Victim.Description: INC targets various sectors, primarily in the United States.
Victim.Industry: Legal Services, Manufacturing, Construction, Technology, Health Care

diamond_model_summary: The INC ransomware group has evolved into a significant threat actor by leveraging the disruption of other ransomware groups to expand its operations. With a focus on sectors like legal services, manufacturing, and healthcare, INC employs advanced techniques such as Rust-based encryptors and credential dumping from Veeam backups. Their infrastructure supports cross-platform attacks, and their motivation is primarily financial, targeting industries where operational downtime pressures victims to pay ransoms.
doc_summary: INC ransomware group has evolved from a nascent ransomware-as-a-service operation to a prolific cybercrime group by 2026, claiming over 830 victims since August 2023. The disruption of LockBit and BlackCat allowed INC to expand as affiliates migrated to alternative ransomware operations. United States organizations account for more than 65% of listed victims, with legal services, manufacturing, construction, technology, and healthcare among the most targeted sectors. INC's Windows and Linux/ESXi encryptors have been rewritten in Rust for cross-platform development and resistance to reverse engineering. The sale of INC's ransomware variants in May 2024 led to related ransomware families like Lynx and Sinobi. INC affiliates use diverse tools and techniques, targeting unpatched edge devices, dumping credentials from Veeam backup servers, and using LOLBins and commercial RMM tools. diamond_model_summary: The ClickFix campaign involves a Russian-speaking adversary targeting macOS users with an AppleScript-based infostealer. The infrastructure includes ClickFix pages masquerading as legitimate utilities, and the victims are primarily in the technology, media, and business services sectors across Asia, North America, and Oceania.
doc_summary: A Russian-speaking attacker has been observed targeting victims mainly in Asia, North America, and Oceania across technology, media, and business services sectors using ClickFix lures to deliver an AppleScript-based infostealer to macOS users. The ClickFix pages masquerade as downloads for a malware scanning utility. To evade detection, the entire infection chain, starting from the initial clipboard paste to payload execution, is completely fileless, leaving no static artifacts on disk until persistence is established. Victims are socially engineered into executing a curl command that fetches a gzip-compressed stager, which pipes the second-stage AppleScript directly into osascript memory. The second-stage, codenamed 'Meow (DEBUG),' uses a fake system dialog to harvest credentials, browser data, session cookies, and keychain contents. It's also equipped with capabilities to trojanize legitimate desktop cryptocurrency wallet applications and maintain persistent command-and-control (C2) access, allowing the operator to run arbitrary payloads.
kill_chain_summary: The ClickFix campaign follows a sophisticated kill chain involving social engineering for delivery, fileless execution for exploitation, and persistence through trojanized cryptocurrency wallets. The adversary maintains command and control via web protocols and achieves their objectives by harvesting credentials and browser data. The attack is characterized by advanced evasion techniques and a focus on macOS users.

doc_summary: Threat actors associated with DragonForce ransomware, identified as Hackledorb, targeted a major United States services firm using a custom Go-based remote access trojan (RAT) called Backdoor.Turn. The attack leveraged Microsoft's TURN relay infrastructure to conceal command-and-control (C2) traffic. Initial access was suspected to be through an SQL or MS-SQL server vulnerability, or possibly via an initial access broker (IAB). The attack began in December 2025, involving a PowerShell command to drop a ZIP archive, leading to a DLL side-loading attack using a Huawei driver. The attackers maintained network presence for one to two months, executing Backdoor.Turn by injecting it into the DbgView64.exe process. The backdoor facilitated command execution, process creation, network scanning, and credential theft. The incident marks the first documented abuse of Microsoft's TURN relay infrastructure by threat actors.

Title: Intrusion into French Automotive Business by Attacker 'Poisson'

Victim.Description: Small French automotive business targeted for credential theft.

diamond_model_summary: The attack on a small French automotive business by 'Poisson' demonstrates a low-sophistication adversary using legitimate tools like OpenSSH and Tailscale for persistence. The attack focused on credential theft, with poor operational security evidenced by leaked SSH keys and exposed directories. The infrastructure relied on free-tier services, and the victim was targeted for financial gain.
doc_summary: A French-speaking attacker, known as 'Poisson', targeted a small French automotive business, deploying a keylogger to steal banking and email credentials. The attacker used OpenSSH and Tailscale to maintain access without relying on the command-and-control (C2) server, which went offline. Cato Networks documented the attack, revealing Poisson's use of tools like DuckDNS, Backblaze B2, and IONOS VPS. The malware operated in memory, using a VBScript stager and PowerShell loader to execute Havoc's Demon agent. Poisson's tradecraft was poor, leaking his home directory and leaving SSH keys exposed. The attack focused on credential theft, with no lateral movement or ransomware. The incident highlights the importance of detecting persistence mechanisms beyond C2 servers.
kill_chain_summary: The attack followed a structured kill chain, starting with the weaponization of a keylogger and memory-resident malware. Delivery was achieved through VBScript and PowerShell loaders. Installation involved OpenSSH and Tailscale for persistence. Command and control were maintained via encrypted channels, and actions on objectives focused on credential theft. The attack highlights the need for detecting persistence mechanisms beyond C2 servers.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes domain names like duckdns.org and tools such as OpenSSH and Tailscale. The attacker's use of legitimate tools complicates detection efforts, emphasizing the need for behavior-based detection. The TTPs employed, including keylogging and encrypted channels, present significant challenges for defenders. The incident underscores the importance of comprehensive threat hunting and detection strategies.

doc_summary: India banned Telegram until June 22 after it was used to sell leaked exam materials. Telegram CEO Pavel Durov accused Indian telecom Reliance of BGP hijacking, affecting users in the United Arab Emirates. The Internet Freedom Foundation criticized the ban as disproportionate. India's Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology invoked Section 69A of the IT Act. Telegram challenged the ban in the Delhi High Court. The disruption extended beyond India, with AS18101 announcing Telegram prefixes. Doug Madory and Anurag Bhatia analyzed the routing issue. The Central Bureau of Investigation arrested individuals involved in the exam fraud. Telegram removed channels sharing leaked materials. The ban impacted students relying on Telegram for NEET exam preparation.

pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes network host artifacts such as BGP announcements and the AS18101 infrastructure. doc_summary: The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has mandated federal agencies to patch a critical vulnerability in the Widget Factory Joomla Content Editor (JCE) plugin. This flaw, actively exploited in the wild, allows unauthorized code execution via low-complexity attacks. The vulnerability stems from improper access control, enabling PHP code upload and execution through new editor profiles for unauthenticated users. The JCE security team released a patch in early June, urging immediate updates due to public exploit code and automated attacks. CISA's Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04 requires federal agencies to secure systems by Friday, emphasizing the risk posed by this frequent attack vector. Agencies must evaluate internet exposure and adhere to patching guidelines. The directive highlights the importance of patching based on exploitation risk, public exposure, automation potential, and control level granted to attackers.
kill_chain_summary: The attack begins with the exploitation of a public-facing application vulnerability in the Joomla JCE plugin, allowing unauthorized code execution. The exploitation stage is critical, as it enables the adversary to gain initial access without authentication. Detection focuses on monitoring unauthorized profile creation and PHP uploads. Remediation involves patching the plugin and conducting thorough malware scans.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident is primarily focused on the TTPs, as the exploitation of the Joomla JCE plugin vulnerability is a key tactic. doc_summary: In June 2026, a significant supply chain attack targeted the Mastra namespace on npm, compromising 144 packages. The attack involved the insertion of a malicious dependency, 'easy-day-js', which acted as a dropper for a cryptocurrency-stealing trojan. The attack was executed by hijacking the npm account 'ehindero', a former Mastra contributor. The malicious package was published by 'sergey2016' and introduced a payload that disabled TLS certificate validation and communicated with C2 servers at '23.254.164.92' and '23.254.164.123'. The attack leveraged Mastra's position in AI and cloud infrastructure, making it a high-value target. The campaign demonstrated advanced techniques, including obfuscated payloads, persistence mechanisms, and cross-platform data exfiltration capabilities. The incident highlighted vulnerabilities in npm's publishing process and the need for stronger provenance and signature verification.
kill_chain_summary: The attack followed a structured kill chain, starting with reconnaissance to identify the Mastra namespace as a target. Weaponization involved cloning the 'dayjs' library to create 'easy-day-js'. Delivery was achieved through npm as a dependency. Exploitation occurred during the npm installation process. Installation involved a background process with persistence. Command and control were maintained via C2 servers. Actions on objectives included stealing cryptocurrency wallet data.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes IP addresses of C2 servers, the 'easy-day-js' tool, and TTPs such as supply chain attacks and obfuscated payload delivery. Title: Malicious Plugins on JetBrains Marketplace Steal AI API Keys

Victim.Description: Developers using the JetBrains Marketplace plugins are targeted.

diamond_model_summary: The incident involves a coordinated malware campaign targeting developers using the JetBrains Marketplace. The adversary's capability includes developing malicious plugins that exfiltrate AI API keys. The infrastructure involves a hardcoded server for data exfiltration. Victims are developers in the software development industry.
doc_summary: Aikido Security discovered a coordinated malware campaign on the JetBrains Marketplace involving at least 15 malicious plugins designed to steal AI API keys from developers. These plugins, acting as AI coding assistants and code-review tools, were published under seven vendor accounts and have been installed nearly 70,000 times. The plugins exfiltrate API keys to a hardcoded server at 39.107.60.51 over HTTP. The campaign began in October 2025, with new plugins published as recently as June 10, 2026. The plugins also offer a paid tier, providing harvested API keys to paying users. BleepingComputer confirmed the presence of credential theft code in the DeepSeek AI Assist plugin. JetBrains has not responded to inquiries about the incident.
kill_chain_summary: The attack follows a structured kill chain: reconnaissance to identify targets, weaponization of plugins, delivery through the JetBrains Marketplace, exploitation upon installation, installation of malicious code, command and control via exfiltration to a remote server, and actions on objectives by stealing and potentially reselling API keys.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes IP addresses and tools as key indicators. The IP address 39.107.60.51 is used for exfiltration, and malicious IDE plugins serve as tools. These indicators are crucial for detection and response efforts, highlighting the adversary's reliance on specific infrastructure and tools.

Title: Malware Distribution via Steam Workshop Wallpaper Engine

Victim.Description: Steam users downloading malicious wallpapers.
Victim.Security_Posture: Vulnerable due to lack of awareness and security measures.

diamond_model_summary: The incident involves threat actors exploiting Steam Workshop to distribute malware via Wallpaper Engine. The adversaries are financially motivated, using the platform's vulnerabilities to hijack accounts, install backdoors, and run cryptomining processes. The infrastructure includes the Steam Workshop, and victims are global Steam users.
doc_summary: Threat actors are exploiting Steam Workshop, a platform for game-related content, to distribute malware through wallpaper packages. These malicious wallpapers can hijack Steam accounts, install backdoors like DarkKomet, and run cryptomining processes. Kaspersky researchers identified the abuse of Wallpaper Engine, which supports executable Windows applications as wallpapers. Malicious files are either bundled directly or hidden in password-protected archives. The malware includes infostealers like Lumma and Vidar, botnet loaders, and ransomware. Despite Valve's removal of identified threats, new submissions are likely. Users are advised to download from trusted sources and use up-to-date antivirus software.
kill_chain_summary: The attack begins with reconnaissance to identify vulnerabilities in Steam Workshop and Wallpaper Engine. Weaponization involves creating malicious wallpaper packages. Delivery occurs through uploading these packages to Steam Workshop. Exploitation leverages Wallpaper Engine's ability to run executables. Installation involves malware like DarkKomet. Command and Control is established for system control, and actions on objectives include account hijacking and cryptomining.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes malware families like DarkKomet, Lumma, and Vidar. The use of Wallpaper Engine as a tool for malware distribution is significant. No specific IP addresses or domains were identified, but the exploitation of Steam Workshop is a key network host artifact. The TTPs involve malware distribution and credential theft.

doc_summary: Rokarolla is a new Android banking trojan targeting 217 banking and cryptocurrency applications. Distributed via malicious websites, it impersonates Google Play Protect and requests accessibility service permissions. The malware communicates with a command-and-control server, sending device profiles to generate unique identifiers for victims. Rokarolla's primary objective is financial data theft, using phishing overlays to steal credentials and credit card information. It employs evasion tactics like disabling Google Play Protect and hiding its icon. Zimperium researchers highlight its extensive command set and administrative control capabilities.

doc_summary: Cybersecurity researchers have identified multiple ClickFix campaigns delivering malware loaders BabaDeda, Lorem Ipsum, and Potemkin. The campaigns highlight the ongoing threat posed by actors like Vanilla Tempest and the impact of Microsoft's disruption of Fox Tempest's malware-signing services.

Title: Pickle in the Middle: Google Cloud Vertex AI SDK Vulnerability

Victim.Description: Victims were users of the Google Cloud Vertex AI SDK who did not set explicit bucket names.
Victim.Security_Posture: Vulnerable due to default SDK settings

diamond_model_summary: The incident involved an adversary exploiting a vulnerability in the Google Cloud Vertex AI SDK to hijack machine learning model uploads. The adversary used predictable bucket names to intercept and replace model uploads, leveraging Google Cloud infrastructure. Victims were users of the SDK who did not set explicit bucket names, leading to unauthorized access to model artifacts and OAuth tokens.
doc_summary: A vulnerability in the Google Cloud Vertex AI SDK for Python allowed attackers to hijack machine learning model uploads without access to the victim's project. Discovered by Palo Alto Networks Unit 42, the flaw, dubbed 'Pickle in the Middle', involved predictable bucket names in Google Cloud Storage. Attackers could create a bucket with the expected name, intercepting model uploads and replacing them with malicious ones. The attack exploited the SDK's default behavior when the staging_bucket parameter was unset. Google patched the issue in version 1.148.0, adding bucket ownership verification. The flaw was reported on March 5, 2026, and no exploitation in the wild was observed. The attack could lead to OAuth token theft and unauthorized access to other model artifacts. Users are advised to update the SDK and set explicit bucket names.
kill_chain_summary: The attack began with reconnaissance to gather public project IDs, followed by weaponization to prepare a malicious model. Delivery involved using a Cloud Function to replace the victim's model upload. Exploitation occurred through predictable bucket naming, leading to installation of the malicious model. Command and control was achieved by executing code to steal OAuth tokens, and actions on objectives involved accessing other model artifacts.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The Pyramid of Pain for this incident includes predictable bucket names as a key indicator. The adversary's use of Google Cloud infrastructure and Cloud Functions are significant tools and techniques. The lack of specific IP addresses, domains, or file hashes limits the ability to track the adversary, but the predictable naming pattern is a critical weakness that was exploited.

Title: GhostTree Technique Exploits NTFS Junctions for Evasion

doc_summary: The GhostTree technique exploits NTFS junctions and symbolic links to create recursive directory loops, allowing attackers to evade detection by endpoint security tools like Windows Defender. This method involves creating junctions that point back to their parent directories, generating infinite file paths that hinder directory scans. The technique, tested against Windows Defender, was reported to Microsoft and subsequently patched. GhostTree highlights the limitations of endpoint scanning and underscores the need for monitoring file system activity at the data layer. The technique's potential impact is significant, as it can render directories unscannable, allowing malicious files to remain undetected.
kill_chain_summary: The GhostTree technique primarily affects the Actions on Objectives stage of the MITRE ATT&CK kill chain. By creating recursive directory loops, attackers can evade detection by endpoint security tools, allowing malicious files to remain undetected. This technique emphasizes the importance of monitoring file system activity to catch what scanners miss.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The GhostTree technique does not rely on specific indicators like hashes or IP addresses, making it challenging to detect using traditional methods. Instead, it exploits NTFS junctions to create recursive loops, highlighting the need for advanced monitoring of file system activity to detect such evasive techniques.

Title: FTC Reports $3.5 Billion Loss to Imposter Scams in 2025

Victim.Description: Individuals in the United States targeted by imposter scams.

diamond_model_summary: The incident involves fraudsters impersonating businesses and government entities to deceive individuals in the United States. The adversaries use social engineering tactics to exploit trust and extract financial information. Social media platforms serve as the primary infrastructure for delivering scams, targeting consumer victims. The impact is significant, with billions lost to these schemes.
doc_summary: The U.S. Federal Trade Commission (FTC) reported that Americans lost $3.5 billion to imposter scams in 2025, with losses nearly tripling since 2020. Imposter scams were the most reported fraud category, accounting for one in three fraud reports. Fraudsters used text messages, phone calls, emails, social media, and search engine results to reach victims. The costliest schemes involved fake bank security alerts prompting fund transfers. Victims lost nearly $1 billion to business impersonators and $920 million to government impersonators. Social media was the most cost-effective attack vector, with $2.1 billion in losses traced to platforms like Facebook, WhatsApp, and Instagram. The FTC has taken enforcement actions, securing over $70 million in consumer redress. Overall fraud losses surged to $16 billion in 2025, the highest on record.
kill_chain_summary: The kill chain involves reconnaissance through social media to gather victim information, weaponization by crafting convincing messages, delivery via communication channels, and exploitation of victim trust to extract financial data. The actions on objectives result in financial gain for the adversaries. Detection and remediation focus on monitoring communication channels and educating users.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: The pyramid of pain for this incident is primarily focused on the use of social engineering tactics and communication platforms. No specific indicators such as hashes, IPs, or domains were identified. The adversaries rely on exploiting human trust, making detection challenging. Remediation efforts should focus on user education and monitoring communication channels for suspicious activity.

It uses a robust C2 infrastructure with multiple fallback domains, making it resilient to takedowns. Victims are Android users with banking and cryptocurrency apps, and the malware exploits Android's Accessibility features for persistence and control.
doc_summary: Security researchers at Zimperium's zLabs have identified a new Android banking trojan named Rokarolla. This malware targets 217 banking and cryptocurrency apps, utilizing 137 remote commands to gain control over infected devices. Rokarolla spreads through malicious websites masquerading as popular apps like TikTok and Chrome. The initial infection vector is a dropper disguised as Google Play Protect, which installs the payload and gains Accessibility access. Rokarolla employs HTML overlays to capture credentials by mimicking legitimate banking app login pages. It also reads and sends SMS, intercepts one-time codes, and rewrites clipboard contents to redirect cryptocurrency payments. The malware uses multiple fallback command-and-control domains, making it resilient to takedowns. Zimperium's products can detect Rokarolla, and indicators of compromise are available in their GitHub repository.
kill_chain_summary: Rokarolla follows a structured kill chain, starting with reconnaissance to identify popular apps to mimic. The weaponization phase involves developing the trojan to exploit Android devices. Delivery occurs via malicious websites posing as legitimate apps. Exploitation involves abusing Android's Accessibility features. Installation ensures persistence by disabling security features. Command and control is maintained through multiple fallback domains. Actions on objectives include credential theft, SMS interception, and cryptocurrency transaction redirection.
pyramid_of_pain_summary: Rokarolla's indicators of compromise include multiple fallback domains and the use of Accessibility features for persistence. The malware's resilience to takedowns is due to its robust C2 infrastructure. While specific hashes, IPs, and domains are not detailed, the malware's behavior and techniques are significant indicators. Rokarolla's use of HTML overlays and SMS interception are key TTPs that contribute to its effectiveness.

doc_summary: Cybersecurity researchers have identified Windows variants of the SprySOCKS backdoor, previously thought to be Linux-only, linked to the FishMonger group, a China-nexus state-sponsored actor. doc_summary: Bad actors are exploiting multiple security vulnerabilities in Fortinet FortiSandbox, according to threat intelligence firm Defused Cyber. The vulnerabilities include CVE-2026-39813, CVE-2026-39808, and CVE-2026-25089, all with a CVSS score of 9.1. CVE-2026-25089, impacting FortiSandbox, FortiSandbox Cloud, and FortiSandbox PaaS WEB UI, was fixed last week. Defused Cyber noted the exploit for CVE-2026-25089 shows signs of AI model development but is faulty. Fortinet released patches for these vulnerabilities in April 2026. Fortinet appliances have been frequent targets, with a critical flaw in FortiClient EMS (CVE-2026-35616) also exploited in the wild.
